What does it cost to install carpet in Newcastle, WA?

Work it from the top down. A main floor of 1,200 sq ft with the staircase attached — the standard Newcastle 90s plan — typically finishes between $5,500 and $8,500, and most projects here total $2,000 to $4,500. Per foot that works out to $4 to $7 installed: carpet, pad, labor, fresh tack strip, haul-away, all of it. Where you land inside the spread is a grade decision, made with full-size samples on your own floor.
Does the mobile carpet showroom really come to Newcastle?

Newcastle sits on our regular route — the Cougar Mountain flank included. Instead of a showroom trip, the van pulls up with 20+ carpet samples aboard, all three pad grades alongside them. We set samples down in the rooms and on the stair treads they'd cover, so the color reads under your own windows, then measure every room and staircase. A written price stays behind, and the visit costs nothing.
What does carpet stretching cost in Newcastle?

Ripples usually mean a hand-stretched install, common in these 90s subdivisions, not carpet that is worn out. A power stretcher pulls waves, bunches and doorway humps flat, starting at $99 per room in Newcastle. New carpet runs about five times that; while the pile has life left and the color still suits the room, stretching is the smarter spend.
How much are carpeted stairs in a Newcastle home?

Stair carpet starts at $18 per step, installed waterfall or cap-and-band. Newcastle's 90s two-stories are full of switchback landings and pie-shaped winder steps, so we count every one in the written quote from the start — nothing surfaces later as an add-on.
How long does a carpet install take in Newcastle?

One day handles most Newcastle houses. Three or four bedrooms plus the staircase is a normal day for the crew; a whole house with heavy furniture and long stair runs can carry into a second day. Your quote spells out the schedule, so there's no guessing on install morning.
Will your installers move my furniture?

Yes — the big pieces are on us. Beds, dressers, couches and tables get moved and set back where they belong once the carpet is in. Your part is the small stuff: closet floors, electronics, lamps, breakables and anything personal you'd rather carry yourself.
Is my carpet worth restretching, or should I replace it?

Three things decide it — backing, pile, color. If the backing holds, the pile springs back, and the color suits the room, a $99-per-room stretch beats buying a new floor; on Newcastle's 90s two-stories the ripples usually show up first in the upstairs hallway. Replace when lanes stay matted, seams pull apart, the backing crackles underfoot, or professional cleaning didn't end the pet smell. We tell you which one you've got before quoting.

What carpet stands up best to pets?

Start underneath. A moisture-barrier pad is what stops an accident from reaching the subfloor, and a soaked subfloor is where odor turns permanent. Over it goes solution-dyed nylon with a sealed backing, its color locked inside the fiber, so even diluted bleach won't lighten it. On the Cougar Mountain side of town, where dogs come home muddy most of the winter, that pairing is worth the $0.65 per square foot the barrier pad adds.
What warranty comes with the install?

Two warranties end up on the same quote. The mill's runs against wear and stain for 10 to 25 years, depending which grade you pick — and on Newcastle's stair-heavy plans the treads are what test it first. Ours is a 1-year workmanship warranty. Both are written down, never just spoken. One catch: mills can tie coverage to a minimum pad grade, which is why all three pad grades ride along to the house.
